analysis.investment_thesis: Power Mech is a capable EPC player riding India's infrastructure wave, but it sits entirely outside my circle of competence and violates my most non-negotiable rules: debt spiked sharply, operating cash flow collapsed to near-zero in FY25 despite ₹348 Cr net profit, and the business model is inherently lumpy and government-dependent. I have built wealth by saying no to businesses I don't understand and cannot predict.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 16% over 9 years with strong recent acceleration (₹3,601 Cr → ₹5,234 Cr in two years)
ROCE of 22.9% is genuinely impressive for a capital-intensive EPC business
Promoter holding at 58.41% is stable and above my 55% floor
key_risks: Debt nearly doubled in one year — borrowings jumped from ₹396 Cr (FY24) to ₹960 Cr (FY25), pushing D/E to 0.41, above my hard limit of 0.3
Operating cash flow collapsed to just ₹1 Cr in FY25 against ₹348 Cr net profit — severe working capital strain signals project execution stress or aggressive revenue recognition
Business recorded a ₹49 Cr net loss in FY21, exposing deep earnings cyclicality tied to government capex cycles — the opposite of what I seek
red_flags: Borrowings nearly 2.5x in a single year (FY24 ₹396 Cr → FY25 ₹960 Cr) — aggressive debt-funded expansion, a pattern I avoid absolutely
OCF of ₹1 Cr in FY25 vs. ₹348 Cr reported profit — cash flow disconnect is the most dangerous signal in any business
FCF turned deeply negative in FY25 (–₹159 Cr) after four consecutive positive years — capex scaling faster than earnings can support
Finance costs have risen steadily from ₹33 Cr to ₹99 Cr over 9 years at 13% CAGR — debt burden compounds alongside business growth
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Power Mech Projects is an EPC contractor serving power, railways, roads, and now renewables — a business model built on project wins, government spending, and working capital cycles. This is fundamentally not a business I would own. I built DMart on predictable daily consumer demand; EPC revenues are lumpy, dependent on government allocations, and subject to execution delays beyond management control. The 2021 loss year (–₹49 Cr net profit) perfectly illustrates what happens when order inflows slow — the fixed cost base crushes margins quickly. The P/E of 22x and P/B of 3.3x are not cheap enough for a cyclical business with these characteristics.

The FY25 numbers are the deciding signal for me. Revenue grew 24% to ₹5,234 Cr and net profit grew 40% to ₹348 Cr — impressive on paper. But operating cash flow was ₹1 Cr. One crore. That tells me the business is growing through working capital — unbilled receivables, retention money locked in projects — and funding it with debt that nearly tripled in one year. Finance costs of ₹99 Cr are now consuming roughly 28% of operating profit. This is the exact pattern of aggressive debt-funded expansion I have always avoided. No dividend discipline, no FCF, rising leverage, and a sector outside my expertise — my answer is clear.
